steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on BlockEcho, a method for imputing block-wise missing data. Motivate the problem, briefly cover existing imputation approaches and where they fall short, explain our idea, and list the contributions and the structure of the paper.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Missing data and matrix completion
  - common in real-world datasets; causes: users reluctant to share, different feature structures, privacy, unintended corruption over time
  - large-scale, highly correlated missing data -> matrix completion to impute unknown entries accurately and efficiently
  - important for dataset analysis, later ML and operations research tasks
  - applications: recommender systems, trajectory recovery, phase retrieval, computer vision, genotype imputation
- Block-wise missing data
  - missing data not only randomly scattered, also in blocks
  - examples: different agents' feature sets -> non-overlapping blocks of NA values when aggregating; skipped clinical trials in some regions (technical, financial constraints); malfunctioning monitoring devices -> continuous corruption
- Existing methods
  - traditional: linear interpolation, KNN imputation, MICE, ensemble methods like MissForest
  - GANs: estimating high-dimensional distributions; recent works use GANs for data recovery
  - most do poorly on block-missing matrices, worse as missing proportion grows
  - rely on neighboring available elements -> vulnerable to systematic feature gaps
  - exception: MF keeps long-range inter-sample dependencies; but linear, misses nonlinear relationships
- BlockEcho
  - combine complementary strengths of GAN and MF, offset limitations
  - MF: explicit long-range inter-element associations; GAN: intrinsic nonlinear patterns
- Contributions
  - analysis + formal definition of "Block-wise" missing data; propose BlockEcho
  - benchmark vs SOTA baselines on public datasets (traffic, epidemiology, recommendations); gains for block-missing and high-rate scattered missing; downstream forecasting
  - theory: global optimality and convergence; synergy of MF (long-range) and GAN (local, complex distributions); rigorous proofs
- Structure
  - Sec 2 literature review; Sec 3 problem definition; Sec 4 BlockEcho; Sec 5 theory; Sec 6 experiments; Sec 7 conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Missing data is a common issue in real-world datasets. It can come from users not wanting to share their data, from differences in feature structures, from privacy concerns, and from data getting corrupted over time by accident. When there is large-scale and highly correlated missing data, matrix completion is needed to impute the unknown entries accurately and efficiently. Estimating the unknown elements of a matrix accurately and efficiently is very important for analysing the dataset, and it also supports later machine learning and operations research tasks. Matrix completion is used in a lot of places, for example recommender systems, trajectory recovery, phase retrieval, computer vision, genotype imputation and other research fields. Missing data is not only randomly scattered elements. It can also happen in blocks, and we call this block-wise missing data. For example, when different agents provide different feature sets, aggregating the data can give non-overlapping blocks of NA values. Also, some regions may skip clinical trials because of technical and financial constraints, and monitoring devices that malfunction can cause continuous data corruption over time.

Many different methods have been developed over the years for the matrix completion problem. They include traditional techniques like linear interpolation, K-nearest neighbors imputation, Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE), and ensemble methods like MissForest. More recently, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have shown great potential for estimating high-dimensional data distributions accurately, so recent works have tried GAN architectures for recovering missing data. But most of the current completion techniques do not work well on block-missing matrices, especially when the missing proportion gets bigger. They mostly use the neighboring available elements to predict the unknown entries, so they are vulnerable when there are systematic feature gaps. Matrix Factorization (MF) is an exception, because it implicitly keeps inter-sample dependencies over longer ranges. But MF assumes linearity, so it cannot capture complex nonlinear relationships. We want to combine the strengths of the two and offset their limitations, so we propose BlockEcho. BlockEcho is an integrated approach for block-missing data that uses the strengths of both GAN and MF. It keeps long-range inter-element associations explicitly with MF and it models intrinsic nonlinear patterns with GANs. Our main contributions are:

- 1. We analyse "Block-wise" missing data in depth and give a formal definition of it. Then we introduce a new solution for this challenge, called BlockEcho.

- 2. We benchmark BlockEcho extensively against SOTA baselines on different public datasets for traffic, epidemiology, and recommendations. The results show significant gains in imputation accuracy for both block-missing data and high-rate scattered missing data. Downstream forecasting tasks also show advantages.

- 3. We give a theoretical analysis of global optimality and convergence for the integrated objective we propose. In particular we justify the synergy between MF encoding long-range dependencies and GANs adapting locally to complex distributions. Rigorous proofs support the empirical observations.

The rest of the paper is organised like this. Section 2 is a short literature review on missing data imputation. Section 3 defines the problem. Section 4 describes our model BlockEcho. Section 5 gives a theoretical discussion. Section 6 has our experiments and results. Section 7 concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Missing data is a prevalent issue in real-world datasets, stemming from factors such as users’ reluctance to share data, variations in feature structures, privacy concerns, and unintended data corruption over time [1]. In scenarios with large-scale and highly correlated missing data, matrix completion becomes essential to impute the unknown entries accurately and efficiently. Accurately and efficiently estimating the unknown elements of a matrix is pivotal for effective dataset analysis and supports subsequent machine learning and operations research tasks. Matrix completion is widely applied in recommender systems, trajectory recovery, phase retrieval, computer vision, genotype imputation and other fields of research [2]. Missing data is not limited to randomly scattered elements; it can also occur in blocks, which we refer to as block-wise missing data. For example, discrepancies in the feature sets provided by different agents can result in non-overlapping blocks of NA values during data aggregation. Moreover, some regions may skip clinical trials due to technical and financial constraints, while malfunctioning monitoring devices can cause continuous data corruption over time.

A wide range of methods have been developed over the years to address the matrix completion problem, from traditional techniques such as linear interpolation, K-nearest neighbors imputation, Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE), to ensemble methods such as MissForest [3]. More recently, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated great potential in accurately estimating high-dimensional data distributions [4], and recent works have therefore explored GAN architectures for data recovery in the missing data context. However, most prevailing completion techniques perform suboptimally on block-missing matrices, especially as the missing proportion increases. They mainly leverage neighboring available elements to predict unknown entries, which makes them vulnerable to systematic feature gaps. An exception is Matrix Factorization (MF), which implicitly retains inter-sample dependencies across longer ranges [5]. Its linearity assumptions, however, limit its ability to capture complex nonlinear relationships. To unite their complementary strengths and offset their limitations, we propose BlockEcho, an integrated approach tailored for block-missing data that capitalizes on the strengths of both GAN and MF. It explicitly retains long-range inter-element associations via MF while modeling intrinsic nonlinear patterns through GANs. The key contributions are:

- 1. We conduct an in-depth analysis and formally define the concept of “Block-wise” missing data. We then introduce a novel solution to this challenge, named BlockEcho.

- 2. We extensively benchmark BlockEcho against SOTA baselines on diverse public datasets for traffic, epidemiology, and recommendations. Results show significant gains in imputation accuracy under both block-missing and high-rate scattered missing regimes. Downstream forecasting tasks further show its advantages.

- 3. We provide a theoretical analysis of global optimality and convergence for the proposed integrated objective. In particular, we justify the synergistic effects of MF encoding long-range dependencies and GANs locally adapting complex distributions. Rigorous proofs supplement the empirical observations.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 provides a concise literature review of missing data imputation studies. Section 3 defines the problem. Section 4 elaborates our model BlockEcho. Section 5 provides a theoretical discussion. Section 6 details our experiments and results. Section 7 concludes the paper.

References:

[2] Santos et al. [2019] Miriam Seoane Santos, Ricardo Cardoso Pereira, Adriana Fonseca Costa, Jastin Pompeu Soares, João Santos, and Pedro Henriques Abreu. Generating synthetic missing data: A review by missing mechanism. IEEE Access , 7:11651–11667, 2019.
[3] Williams [2015] R Williams. Missing data part 1: Overview, traditional methods. university of notre dame, 2015.
